questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Matrix Multiplication
questions.problem:
Given that $A,B,$ and $C$ are $6\times 6$ matrices which of the following statements are always true? 

- $CB=BC$
- $A(B-C)=AB-CA$
- $A(BC)=(AB)C$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

- Statement I is false. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so $AB\ne BA$ in general.

- Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $A(B-C)=AB-AC,$ but $AC\ne CA$ because matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is associative and  $A(BC)=(AB)C$ is always true.

Therefore, only statement  III is true.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Matrix Multiplication
questions.problem:
Given that $A,B,$ and $C$ are $7\times 7$ matrices which of the following statements are always true? 

- $(CA)B=C(BA)$
- $(A+A)B=2AB$
- $CB=BC$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

- Statement I  is false. Matrix multiplication is associative and  $(CA)B=C(AB)$ is always true. However,  matrix multiplication is not commutative,   $AB\ne BA$ in general. Therefore, $(CA)B\ne C(BA)$ in general.

- Statement II is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $(A+A)B=AB+AB=2AB$ is always true.

- Statement III is false. Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general, so $CB\ne BC$ in general.

Therefore, only statement II is true.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Associative Law
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall the associative law

$$
ABC=(AB)C=A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix, $B$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix, and $C$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $2\times 1$ matrix, which will require finding $2$ entries, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $3\times 2$ matrix, which will require finding $6$ entries.

So, we find the product $AB$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $AB$ by $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =(AB)C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-11 & 11 \\ -8 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Associative Law
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall the associative law

$$
ABC=(AB)C=A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix, $B$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix, and $C$ is a $2\times 1$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $3\times 2$ matrix, which will require finding $6$ entries, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $1\times 1$ matrix, which will require finding only $1$ entry.

So, we find the product $BC$ first: 

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-20-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-26\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $A$ by $BC:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =A(BC) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-26\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}78 \\ -52 \\ -182\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
